item.title: Overnight strikes in Yemen kill at least 1 person and wound 9, and other Mideast news
item.description:
Overnight strikes in Yemen kill at least 1 person and wound 9, and other Mideast news
Overnight strikes in Yemen have hit a gas station and an oil facility, killing at least one person and wounding nine othersByThe Associated PressNovember 10, 2026, 7:06 AM
Share
Overnight strikes hit a gas station and an oil facility in Yemen, killing at least one person and wounding nine, residents and the Iran-backed Houthi rebels said on Tuesday.
In Iran, a top security official claimed that the Iran war had already “wrecked” the United States, and called on Washington to accept seven demands that Tehran has made for an end to the conflict.
Here is the latest news from the Middle East on Tuesday. Read our full coverage here.
Houthi-run health ministry spokesperson Anees al-Asbahi said in a statement on X on Tuesday that a strike hit a gas station in a district of Yemen's capital, Sanaa, killing one person and wounding three others.
He said another airstrike targeted an oil company, wounding at least six people, causing “extensive damage” to nearby homes and shops and panicking residents.
Al-Asbahi blamed Saudi Arabia for both strikes. The Associated Press couldn’t independently verify his claims.
The strikes come amid renewed fighting between the Houthis and Saudi-backed government forces that escalated this summer. The rebels continue to target Saudi energy facilities and airports as part of a campaign they say is meant to push Saudi Arabia into lifting its blockade on Yemen.
Sanaa resident Khaled al-Khawlani told the AP on Tuesday that he was horrified by the explosions that targeted the oil facility near residential areas of Sanaa at around 4 a.m.
Another resident said the explosions shattered his windows and reverberated across the city while people slept. The resident spoke on condition of anonymity for security reasons.

item.title: Islamic State group-affiliated rebels kill at least 22 in Congo's eastern region
item.description:
Islamic State group-affiliated rebels kill at least 22 in Congo's eastern region
A rebel group affiliated with the Islamic State group has killed at least 22 people in Congo's eastern Ituri provinceByJEAN-YVES KAMALE Associated Press and JUSTIN KABUMBA Associated PressNovember 11, 2026, 11:52 AM
ITURI, Congo -- At least 22 people were killed in a series of attacks by a rebel group affiliated with the Islamic State group between Tuesday and Wednesday in Congo 's eastern Ituri province.
The attacks were carried out by the Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) across eight locations in the Mambasa territory in Ituri, according to two civil society and human rights monitoring groups.
At least 10 people were also abducted.
“The death toll remains provisional. In addition to the 22 civilians killed, the perpetrators abducted other individuals, and motorcycles and homes were set on fire,” said Marie-Noelle Anatobe, coordinator of the Civil Society of Congo in Mambasa territory.
The attacks happened in nearly inaccessible locations near the border between Uganda and Congo.
The ADF grew out of Uganda and was pushed to the border region with Congo, where it has operated for years, targeting civilians. It pledged allegiance to the Islamic State group in 2019.
Both the Ugandan and Congolese armies have been jointly attacking the group, but they have long struggled against it.

item.title: Spain holds state funeral for 69 killed in high-speed rail crash
item.description:
Spain holds state funeral for 69 killed in high-speed rail crash
Relatives of the 69 people killed in a high-speed rail collision in Spain last month attended a state funeral TuesdayByFRANCISCO SECO Associated Press and SUMAN NAISHADHAM Associated PressNovember 10, 2026, 2:16 PM
TOLEDO, Spain -- Relatives of the 69 people killed in a high-speed rail collision in Spain last month attended a state funeral on Tuesday with Spain's royals, almost two weeks after the crash.
The ceremony took place in the towering 13th-century Toledo Cathedral in central Spain.
The collision happened on Oct. 28 when a high-speed train slammed into another that was stationary on the Madrid-Seville line near Urda, around 140 kilometers (87 miles) south of the capital.
It was the second deadly collision this year involving Spain’s extensive high-speed rail network, shattering Spaniards' trust in the transit system that is regarded as one of the country's crowning achievements.
Under growing pressure, Transport Minister Óscar Puente stepped down last week. His resignation was followed by that of Luis Pedro Marco, who was head of Spain's railway infrastructure operator.
Spain will hold a general election on Nov. 29, in which progressive Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez is seeking reelection.
Sánchez did not attend Tuesday's funeral service.
A 16th-century sculpture of Christ was moved from the town of Urda to the cathedral in Toledo for the funeral service.

item.title: China and ASEAN make progress on South China Sea pact but can't finish talks this year
item.description:
China and ASEAN make progress on South China Sea pact but can't finish talks this year
Regional diplomats say China and Southeast Asian countries have made progress on a South China Sea pact but won’t be able to conclude negotiations this year as agreedByJIM GOMEZ Associated PressNovember 10, 2026, 10:01 PM
MANILA, Philippines -- China and Southeast Asian countries have made progress on a South China Sea pact but won't be able to conclude decades of negotiations this year as agreed, three regional diplomats said Wednesday.
China and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations began negotiating the so-called “code of conduct” in 2005 to prevent occasional confrontations in the disputed waters from turning into a major conflict that could threaten Asia’s economies. The accord mainly calls for self-restraint and discourages aggressive acts that could spark clashes in the waterway that is a key global trade route.
After years of closed-door negotiations, which at times were delayed due to tense clashes in the contested waters, China and ASEAN agreed in 2023 to speed up the negotiations and conclude the talks by this year.
Three senior Southeast Asian diplomats with direct knowledge of the negotiations told The Associated Press that after the final round of this year's talks last month, China and the ASEAN have provisionally agreed on about 80% of all the paragraphs that will be included in the agreement.
The last major sticking points are the geographic scope to be covered by the agreement, the definition of sensitive terms and whether the accord should be legally binding or not, according to the three diplomats. They spoke on condition of anonymity and without elaborating because they were not authorized to discuss the issues in public.

item.title: Militants ambush police vehicles in northwestern Pakistan, killing at least 10 officers
item.description:
Militants ambush police vehicles in northwestern Pakistan, killing at least 10 officers
Police say militants have ambushed vehicles carrying police officers in northwestern Pakistan, triggering a gunbattle that killed at least 10 officersByThe Associated PressNovember 11, 2026, 6:26 AM
PESHAWAR, Pakistan -- PESHAWAR, Pakistan (AP) — Militants ambushed vehicles carrying police officers in northwestern Pakistan on Wednesday, triggering a gunbattle that killed at least 10 officers, officials said.
The attack took place in Kohat, a district in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, which borders Afghanistan, local police official Faisal Khan said.
He said two senior police officers were among the dead and an exchange of fire between security forces and the attackers was ongoing He provided no further details.
No group immediately claimed responsibility, but suspicion is likely to fall on the Pakistani Taliban, known as Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan, or TTP, which has stepped up attacks on security forces in the region in recent months.

item.title: Austria tightens laws against spying to protect the international organizations it hosts
item.description:
Austria tightens laws against spying to protect the international organizations it hosts
Austria has launched plans to tighten its espionage laws, which currently only ban spying against Austria itselfByGEIR MOULSON Associated PressNovember 11, 2026, 8:04 AM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
BERLIN -- Austria's government on Wednesday launched plans to tighten the country's laws against spying, which at present explicitly ban espionage directed against Austria itself but not if it targets other countries or international organizations.
Austria is a European Union member that has a policy of military neutrality dating back to the 1950s. Its capital, Vienna, is host to several U.N. agencies including the International Atomic Energy Agency. It is also the home of other international groups such as the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe and the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries, or OPEC.
“Espionage is a real threat to our security, to security in our country, but above all to our reputation as Austria, as the capital of dialogue, as an official location of the U.N. and over 40 international organizations,” Foreign Minister Beate Meinl-Reisinger said as Cabinet ministers presented the draft legislation. “We have a responsibility ... and we are fulfilling this responsibility.”
Meinl-Reisinger acknowledged that Vienna has often been described as a “capital of espionage,” a reputation dating back to the Cold War, but said she wants to dispense with any “romantic idea” of spying.
She said that “we are responding to the current hybrid threat situation.” That's a term for non-conventional hostile acts such as sabotage, cyberattacks, disinformation and an array of other methods.

item.title: Pope Leo XIV wrapping up Argentina visit before an emotional trip back to Peru, his adopted homeland
item.description:
Pope Leo XIV wrapping up Argentina visit before an emotional trip back to Peru, his adopted homeland
Pope Leo XIV is wrapping up his visit to Argentina with two poignant momentsByNICOLE WINFIELD Associated Press and DÉBORA REY Associated PressNovember 11, 2026, 4:18 AM
Share
BUENOS AIRES, Argentina -- BUENOS AIRES, Argentina (AP) — Pope Leo XIV told inmates at an Argentine prison with a dark history tied to the military dictatorship that there is always hope for redemption and reconciliation, as he spent his final morning in Argentina on Wednesday offering an uplifting message to a polarized country.
Leo visited Devoto Prison before celebrating his final Mass at Argentina’s national shrine, the Basilica de Nuestra Señora de Luján, where 1 million people were expected — the latest of the record-setting crowds that have welcomed Leo on the first papal visit to Argentina in nearly four decades.
Both sites have important sentimental connections to Leo’s predecessor, Pope Francis, who never returned home during his 12-year pontificate. But Leo’s final stops in Argentina pale in comparison to the emotional highlight of his South American trip, when he returns to his adopted homeland of Peru later Wednesday.
A massive national party is planned to greet the Chicago-born Leo, who spent more than two decades as a missionary priest and bishop in Peru and holds dual citizenship in the United States and Peru. He’s known to Peruvians as Padre Robert and beloved for ministering to poor communities, especially in times of crisis.
In Buenos Aires, Leo visited Devoto Prison, where Francis often ministered as the city’s archbishop, celebrating Mass, going into cellblocks housing inmates with AIDS and washing prisoners’ feet during the annual Holy Week ritual.

item.title: Nigerian court orders journalist kept in custody, renewing concerns over freedom
item.description:
Nigerian court orders journalist kept in custody, renewing concerns over freedom
A decision by a court in Nigeria to keep investigative journalist Daniel Ojukwu in custody has sparked renewed concerns about media freedomByDYEPKAZAH SHIBAYAN Associated PressNovember 11, 2026, 8:27 AM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
ABUJA, Nigeria -- A decision by a court in Nigeria to keep an investigative journalist in custody has sparked widespread outrage, renewing concerns about media freedom in the country.
Daniel Ojukwu, with the Foundation for Investigative Journalism, or FIJ, a local investigative media house, was jailed on a 12-count charge for allegedly violating the country’s cybercrime act, pending a bail hearing. The court's decision was issued on Tuesday.
The law has long been seen as a tool to censor journalists in Nigeria, where journalists are exposed to political persecution over reports.
Nigeria is ranked 112th out of 180 countries in the 2026 World Press Freedom Index published by Reporters Without Borders — only improving by 10 places since 2025.
At least 29 journalists have faced prosecution under Nigeria’s cybercrimes law since it was enacted in 2015, the Committee to Protect Journalists said in a report in October 2024.
Ojukwu was arrested for a report on the alleged financial mismanagement of more than 147 million naira ($109,000) involving a senior government official, according to the charge sheet seen by The Associated Press. The case was filed by the office of the Inspector-General of Police.

item.title: Indonesia's vice president offers resignation as questions mount over his eligibility
item.description:
Indonesia's vice president offers resignation as questions mount over his eligibility
Indonesia’s Vice President Gibran Rakabuming Raka has offered to resign amid mounting pressure over his academic credentials, officials sayByNINIEK KARMINI Associated Press and EDNA TARIGAN Associated PressNovember 10, 2026, 7:00 AM
JAKARTA, Indonesia -- Indonesia's vice president offered to resign during a meeting with President Prabowo Subianto on Tuesday, according to officials, adding to the turmoil at the highest levels of the country's leadership.
Vice President Gibran Rakabuming Raka, the 39-year-old son of former President Joko Widodo, held over two hours of talks with Prabowo, according to State Secretariat Minister Prasetyo Hadi.
It was not immediately clear whether Prabowo accepted the resignation, Hadi told reporters at a news conference at the presidential palace. The president advised Raka to “continue pursuing legal avenues to defend the validity of his academic documents,” Hadi said.
As he left his office later in the day, Raka made a brief statement to reporters without addressing the resignation offer.
“I respect all criticism and feedback from the public regarding the developments that are taking place,” Raka said. “I do not want the current situation to become a prolonged political controversy.”
The resignation offer comes amid growing pressure on Raka over a court dispute involving his academic credentials. It was apparently not related to an ongoing probe into allegations that top police officials, including the president's chief of staff Gen. Listyo Sigit Prabowo, had been involved in a wiretap targeting the president. Three other police generals have also been implicated in the case.
Listyo previously served as national police chief under Widodo, who has not been implicated in the wiretapping investigation.

item.title: Dominican president says he backs Bukele and Salvadoran troops in Haiti
item.description:
Dominican president says he backs Bukele and Salvadoran troops in Haiti
The president of the Dominican Republic says his government is collaborating with El Salvador’s president and providing him with logistics and intelligence as some 2,500 troops from the Central American country battle violent gangs in HaitiByDÁNICA COTO Associated PressNovember 10, 2026, 4:54 PM
SAN JUAN, Puerto Rico -- The president of the Dominican Republic said Tuesday that his government is collaborating with El Salvador’s president and providing him with logistics and intelligence as some 2,500 troops from the Central American country battle violent gangs in Haiti.
Dominican President Luis Abinader spoke as the operations of the recently deployed Salvadoran troops to Haiti draw scrutiny because they are largely operating outside the framework of a U.N.-backed, multinational gang suppression force.
Abinader called on the gang suppression force to coordinate its actions with El Salvador’s troops to “decisively support the Salvadoran military and the attitude of President Bukele.”
Igor Rugwiza, spokesperson for the gang suppression force, told The Associated Press on Tuesday that it is coordinating closely with Haitian authorities and relevant international partners “in support of shared security objectives.”
“The (force) considers effective coordination and deconfliction among all security actors operating in Haiti to be essential to achieving sustainable security outcomes,” he said in a statement.
Rugwiza added that any activity undertaken by the force “is conducted in accordance with its mandate, established command and control arrangements, the rules of engagement, and applicable human rights law obligations.”
Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele recently celebrated an attack carried out by Haitian police and Salvadoran troops that destroyed the home of Wilson Joseph, best known as Lanmò San Jou and leader of the 400 Mawozo gang. He was not killed in Sunday’s attack.
